questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD basics: ConfigMap-driven content, Pod specs with probes, RBAC-lite concepts via namespace policies, and basic networking isolation.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap as volume source for static content
- Pod readiness/liveness probes
- Resource requests/limits
- ConfigMap-driven rolling updates via annotation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: site-content
data:
  index.html: |-
    <html><body>Hello</body></html>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-site
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: static-site
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        site-content-hash: "<hash>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: site-content
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: site-content
        configMap:
          name: site-content
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate updating the site content without full redeploys?
- What are the trade-offs of using a ConfigMap for large HTML content?

Why This Is Asked

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
CKAD requires practical mastery of node-scoped components, DaemonSets, hostPath volumes, and real-world log shipping patterns.

## Key Concepts
- DaemonSet on each node with hostPath volumes
- Log tailing with tail -F and sidecar shipping
- ConfigMap-driven batching (BATCH_SIZE)
- NodeSelector to target workers
- Readiness/Liveness probes and lifecycle (preStop)
- Resource requests/limits and rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-collector
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log | /usr/local/bin/shipper --endpoint http://log-portal:5000/api/v1/logs --batch-size $(BUS_BATCH)" ]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
          type: Directory
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under burst log loads and verify end-to-end delivery? 
- How would you rollback a DaemonSet rollout if a regression is found?

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: namespace-audit
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: auditor-sa
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:latest

              image: audit-runner:latest

          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret integration, InitContainer tooling, PVC-backed logs, custom metrics exposure, readiness/liveness, HPA kinship, minimal YAML.

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: feature-tester
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: feature-tester
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: feature-tester
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache httpie jq && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: tester
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do for url in $(cat /etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints); do resp=$(http --ignore-stdin GET "$url" Authorization:"Bearer $(cat /secret/api_token)"); echo "$url -> $resp" >> /logs/$(date +%s).log; done; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: ENDPOINTS_CONFIG
          value: "/etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints"
        - name: TOKEN_SECRET
          valueFrom:

        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs

        - containerPort: 8080

        livenessProbe:

            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"

        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: feature-tester-logs
      - name: feature-endpoints
        configMap:
          name: feature-endpoints
      - name: secret
        secret:
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical Kubernetes operational skills including StatefulSet storage migration, configuration change propagation, health monitoring, security hardening, and availability guarantees during disruptions.

## Key Concepts
- PersistentVolumeClaim integration with StatefulSets and StorageClass selection
- ConfigMap checksum annotations for automated rolling updates
- Health probe configuration (readiness vs liveness)
- Pod security context with non-root execution and file system permissions
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintaining service availability
- Load testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Strategic merge patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/collector
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/collector
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: collector-config
          items:
          - key: config
            path: config
        annotations:
          checksum/config: "{{ .Values.configChecksum }}"
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: "fast-ssd"
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Verification Strategy
Monitor rollout progress: `kubectl rollout status statefulset/collector -n telemetry`
Validate pod health: `kubectl get pods -n telemetry -l app=collector -w`
Check PVC binding: `kubectl get pvc -n telemetry`
Load test using k6 or hey targeting collector endpoints
Verify ConfigMap changes trigger restarts by updating ConfigMap and watching pod recreation

## Rollback Approach
Use `kubectl rollout undo statefulset/collector -n telemetry` for immediate rollback
For complex issues, restore from previous StatefulSet manifest and scale down/up
Always validate PDB compliance during rollback to avoid availability violations

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to compose CKAD primitives into a small, observable application with proper security and observability patterns.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration management
- InitContainers and Sidecars for application lifecycle management
- Probes (readiness and liveness) for health monitoring
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for traffic security
- RBAC basics for in-namespace metrics access
- Observability and security trade-offs in containerized applications

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Deployment sketch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: python-api
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: python-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: python-api
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-deps
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'pip install -r /app/requirements.txt']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['python', '/app/main.py']
        env:
        - name: ENABLE_METRICS
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: ENABLE_METRICS
        - name: API_USERNAME
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: username
        - name: API_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: password
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      - name: cert-rotator
        image: cert-manager/cert-manager-rotator:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /etc/certs
      volumes:
      - name: app-code
        configMap:
          name: app-code
      - name: certs
        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000
```

## Trade-offs
- **Security vs. Complexity**: NetworkPolicy adds security but increases deployment complexity
- **Resource Overhead**: Sidecar containers double resource requirements for cert management
- **Observability Cost**: Metrics endpoint requires additional monitoring infrastructure
- **InitContainer Impact**: Dependency installation extends pod startup time
- **Namespace Isolation**: Per-namespace design improves security boundaries but requires duplicate configuration management

Tests knowledge of Namespace-scoped quotas and defaults, a core CKAD topic. It also checks YAML correctness and practical validation steps.

## Key Concepts

- ResourceQuota structure and hard limits
- LimitRange defaults and constraints
- Impact on deployments and pod scheduling
- Validation commands and monitoring

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "20"
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-a-defaults
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "128Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "50m"
      memory: "64Mi"
    type: Container
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: quiz-app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: quiz-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: quiz-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:stable-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adjust quotas for a namespace that periodically spikes usage?
- What are risks of defaulting too low on requests in LimitRange?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests ConfigMap usage, file-based config in a mounted volume, and in-app dynamic behavior without restarts. Checks readiness/liveness best practices and basic NetworkPolicy scoping.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps mounted as files
- Polling for dynamic config reload
- Readiness and liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: flags-config
  namespace: default
data:
  flags.json: |
    {"enableFeature": true}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-tester
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-tester
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-tester
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: your-registry/flag-tester:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: flags
          mountPath: /etc/flags/flags.json
          subPath: flags.json
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: flags
        configMap:
          name: flags-config
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you test config-change reload without pod restart?
- What limitations exist with polling vs. watching a ConfigMap mount?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests real-world container orchestration patterns: InitContainers for bootstrap, sidecar for log shipping, shared volumes for cross-container data, and proper health checks plus rollback strategy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for pre-boot config
- Shared volumes and proper MountPaths
- Sidecar pattern for log shipping
- Readiness and Liveness probes tailored to production workloads
- Rollback strategy and safe deploys

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch sketch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: processor
  namespace: payments
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fix-permissions
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "chown -R 1000:1000 /mnt/logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /mnt/logs
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: your-registry/processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: in-data
          mountPath: /data/input
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/processor
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
      - name: log-shipper
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /var/log/processor/app.log | nc log-collector 10514"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/processor
        - name: ship
          mountPath: /var/log/ship
      volumes:
      - name: in-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: processor-input-pvc
      - name: logs
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: ship
        emptyDir: {}
      restartPolicy: Always
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate zero-downtime rollouts with this setup? 
- How would you monitor and retry failed log shipments without impacting processor throughput?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of Kubernetes resource governance and multi-tenant fairness in CKAD context.

## Key Concepts
- ResourceQuota HARD and scoped quotas
- LimitRange min/max and defaults
- Namespace scoping and validation
- Troubleshooting quotas with kubectl events

## Code Example
```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev

# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: dev-quota
spec:
  hard:
    pods: 5
    requests.cpu: '1'
    requests.memory: '1Gi'
    limits.cpu: '2'
    limits.memory: '2Gi'

# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: dev-limit
spec:
  limits:
  - max:
      cpu: '500m'
      memory: '512Mi'
    min:
      cpu: '100m'
      memory: '128Mi'
    type: Container

# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: '200m'
            memory: '256Mi'
          limits:
            cpu: '300m'
            memory: '256Mi'
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you alert on quota utilization changes?
- What happens if a user legitimately needs more capacity?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests RBAC scoping, CronJob scheduling, and in-cluster data backup to a ConfigMap without leaking secrets.

## Key Concepts
- RBAC granularity scoped to a namespace
- CronJob scheduling and Job templates
- Reading Kubernetes events via API in-cluster
- Updating/creating a ConfigMap from a Job

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: events-backup-sa
  namespace: metrics
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: events-backup-role
  namespace: metrics
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["events"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get","update","create","patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: events-backup-binding
  namespace: metrics
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: events-backup-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: events-backup-sa
  namespace: metrics
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: events-backup
  namespace: metrics
spec:
  schedule: "*/2 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: events-backup-sa
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","kubectl get events -n metrics -o json | jq '.items[0:50]' > /backup/events.json; kubectl create configmap events-backup --from-file=events.json=/backup/events.json -n metrics --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: backup
            emptyDir: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor the ConfigMap growth and avoid hitting 1MiConfigMap limit?
- How would you rollback if the CronJob misbehaves or RBAC scope expands unintentionally?
